topics.title: Location of Our District in Uganda
topics.heading: TOPIC 1: LOCATION OF OUR DISTRICT IN UGANDA

blocks.x: *Curriculum reference: NCDC Primary Four Social Studies Syllabus, Term I, Topic 1 (16 periods, pages 17–20).*
**How to use this topic.** The syllabus is about **your own district** — every learner is in a different district. Where you see a blank like *(your district)*, write in your own answer.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: name the points of the compass
find your district on the map of Uganda
name the sub-counties, counties and municipalities in your district
name the districts that neighbour yours
compare the size of your district with its neighbours
name important places in your district

blocks.x: A district is a **large part of Uganda with its own local government**. Uganda is divided into **districts** so that government can bring services nearer to the people.
**Note from the syllabus:** counties are **not** part of the main administrative structure of every district. In some places they exist and in others they do not.

**Newer than the syllabus:** this syllabus was written in **2010**, when Uganda had far fewer districts. New districts have been created many times since then, and the number is now **over 130**. Different sources give slightly different totals because new districts keep being added. **Ask your teacher for the number this year** — do not learn an old number by heart.

sections.title: 2. Name the parts of a district, from the biggest to the smallest.

Meaning

blocks.x: You are **not** asked to learn every sub-county by heart. The syllabus says you should know **the ones near you** and be able to find the rest by asking or by reading a map.
A compass is an **instrument that shows direction**.
The four cardinal points are **North, East, South and West**.

NORTH
                   |
                   |
    WEST ----------+---------- EAST
                   |
                   |
                 SOUTH
**A way to remember them, going clockwise from the top:** **N**ever · **E**at · **S**our · **W**atermelon → **N, E, S, W**.
The semi-cardinal points lie **between** the cardinal points.

sections.title: 6. How can you find direction without a compass?

head: Way
How it works
rows: The sun rises in the **East** and sets in the **West**
In the morning shadows point **west**; in the evening they point **east**
Face the sunrise: in front is East, behind is West, your left hand is North and your right hand is South

The one that measures longer is the **bigger** district.
Use the map **scale** to change your measurement into real kilometres.

topics.subject: SST
topics.title: Physical Features in Our District
topics.heading: TOPIC 2: PHYSICAL FEATURES IN OUR DISTRICT

blocks.x: *Curriculum reference: NCDC Primary Four Social Studies Syllabus, Term I, Topic 2 (20 periods, pages 20–23).*

**How to use this topic.** The syllabus asks about the physical features of **your own district**. These notes teach you what each feature is, what it is used for and how to care for it. You then name the ones found in your district.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: say what physical features are
name the physical features found in your district and locate them on a map
explain the uses of physical features
explain the dangers of some physical features
suggest ways of caring for physical features

blocks.x: **Physical features** are the **natural things on the earth's surface** — things that were not made by people.
A **dam** is listed in the syllabus with lakes because a dam holds water like a lake — but remember a dam is **built by people**, while a lake is natural.

sections.title: 2. Name the physical features in the syllabus and what each one is.

head: Feature
What it is
rows: Water flowing in a channel from a highland to a lake or sea
A large body of water surrounded by land
A wall built across a river to hold back water
Raised land, lower than a mountain
Very high raised land, often with a rocky top
Low land lying between hills or mountains
A very long, deep, wide valley formed when the land sank between cracks

blocks.x: **Others you may see in your district:** swamps, forests, islands, waterfalls, rocks and springs.
**Fill this in for your own district**
A swamp is **wet land covered with water and water plants**.

sections.title: 4. What are physical features used for?

blocks.x: Physical features are **natural resources which people use to earn a living**.

head: Feature
How people use it
rows: Fishing · water for drinking, washing and animals · transport by boat · irrigation · tourism
Storing water · making electricity · watering animals
Quarrying stones · growing crops on the slopes · tourism and climbing · rain formation
Growing crops such as rice · grazing animals · settlement
Farming · grazing cattle · building homes, roads and towns
Papyrus for mats and baskets · clay for bricks and pots · growing yams and rice · home for birds and fish
Timber · firewood · herbs for medicine · homes for animals · rainfall

sections.title: 5. What dangers come from physical features?

blocks.x: Physical features are useful, but they can also cause harm.

head: Feature
Danger
rows: **Drowning** · floods · dangerous animals such as crocodiles and hippos · water-borne diseases such as bilharzia and cholera
Mosquitoes that spread **malaria** · people can sink and drown
Dangerous animals and snakes · people get lost · bush fires

sections.title: 6. How can we keep safe near physical features?

items: Do not swim in a lake or river without a grown-up who can swim.
Do not build a house at the bottom of a very steep slope.
Sleep under a **treated mosquito net** if you live near a swamp.
Do not enter a forest alone.
**If you see someone in danger, call an adult at once. Do not jump into the water yourself.**

sections.title: 7. How do we care for physical features?

head: Feature
How to care for it
rows: Do not throw rubbish in the water · do not wash cars or bathe in the source · leave plants growing on the banks · do not fish with poison or small nets
Fence them · keep animals away · keep the surroundings clean
Plant trees and grass · dig **terraces** and trenches across the slope · do not cut all the trees
Do not drain the whole swamp · harvest papyrus carefully and let it grow again
Plant more trees · cut only mature trees · avoid bush burning
Practise **crop rotation** and mulching · avoid over-grazing

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Protecting something so that it lasts
Planting trees where there were none
Planting trees again where they were cut
Cutting down trees and not replacing them
The carrying away of soil by water or wind
Cutting steps across a slope to stop the soil washing away

sections.title: 9. How do physical features affect people?

items: People **settle** where there is water and good flat land, so plains and lake shores are crowded.
People **avoid** very steep slopes, very dry places and big swamps, so these have few people.
Physical features decide the **work** people do — fishing at a lake, farming on a plain, quarrying on a hill.
Mountains **help rain to form**, so their slopes are usually green and good for crops.
Rivers and lakes can be **boundaries** between districts.
Calling a road, a bridge or a building a physical feature.
Saying a hill and a mountain are the same — a **mountain is much higher**.
Giving a **use** when the question asks for a **danger**.
Writing "cutting trees" as a way of **caring** for a forest.
Mixing up **afforestation** (planting new) with **reafforestation** (planting again).
Naming a feature that is not in your own district.

**Natural things found on the earth's surface** that were not made by people.
Any four of **hills, mountains, valleys, plains, rivers, lakes, swamps, forests, rocks, islands**

**Water flowing in a channel** from a highland to a lake or sea
**Low land lying between hills or mountains**
**Flat or gently sloping land**

**Malaria**
Any three of **do not throw rubbish in it, do not fish with poison, leave plants on the banks, do not use small nets, do not bathe or wash cars at the source**
**Cutting steps across a slope to stop soil being washed away**
**The carrying away of soil by water or wind**
**Afforestation** is planting trees where there were none; **deforestation** is cutting down trees without replacing them.
Because the land is **flat and easy to farm and build on**, and there is usually water.

blocks.x: *Curriculum reference: NCDC Primary Four Social Studies Syllabus, Term II, Topic 3 (25 periods, pages 23–26).*
**How to use this topic.** The syllabus asks about the vegetation of **your own district**. You name the types of vegetation found where you live.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: say what vegetation is
name the types of vegetation
tell natural vegetation from planted vegetation
give the uses of vegetation
name the activities of people that damage vegetation
suggest ways of caring for vegetation

blocks.x: **Vegetation** means **all the plants growing in a place**. It is sometimes called the **land cover**, because plants cover the land.
Vegetation includes big trees, small trees, bushes, grass and even the plants growing in water.

sections.title: 2. Name the five types of vegetation.

head: Type
What it looks like
rows: Many tall trees growing close together, with thick shade
Wet land covered with water plants such as papyrus and reeds
Short woody plants and bushes, shorter than trees
Land covered mainly with grass, with a few scattered trees
Plants that people have planted for food or for sale

sections.title: 3. What is the difference between natural and planted vegetation?

head: **Natural vegetation**
**Planted vegetation**
rows: People weed, prune and water it
Natural forest, natural swamp, wild grassland, bushes
A pine or eucalyptus plantation, a banana garden, a tea or sugar-cane estate, trees planted at school

blocks.x: **A quick test:** if the trees stand in **straight rows**, people planted them.

sections.title: 4. What are the uses of vegetation?

head: Use
How it helps
rows: Many local medicines come from leaves, roots and bark
Fruits, vegetables, mushrooms, honey and yams
Plants give out the oxygen we breathe
Trees give off water vapour, which helps rain to form
Roots hold the soil; trees act as a windbreak
Trees, flowers and lawns make a place look good

blocks.x: **More uses you should also know**

items: **Timber** for building and furniture
**Shade** for people and animals
**Grazing** — grass feeds cattle, sheep and goats
**Homes for wild animals, birds and insects**
**Tourism** — visitors pay to see forests and the animals in them
**Materials** — papyrus for mats and baskets, reeds for roofing, bark for crafts

sections.title: 5. Which activities of people damage vegetation?

head: Activity
What it does
rows: Kills small plants, insects and young trees
Uses up the soil so plants can no longer grow well
Too many animals eat the grass down to the roots
Cutting down trees without replacing them
Clearing swamps and burning firewood to bake the bricks
Trees and grass are cleared for the road
Land is cleared for homes and factories

sections.title: 6. What happens when vegetation is destroyed?

items: **Soil erosion** — nothing holds the soil, so rain washes it away
**Less rain** — fewer trees means less water vapour in the air
**Drought** and dry streams
**Wild animals lose their homes**
**Shortage of firewood, timber and herbs**
Strong winds blow off roofs because there is no windbreak
**Deserts** can form where the land is left bare

sections.title: 7. How do we care for vegetation?

head: Way
What to do
rows: Plant trees where there were none
Plant trees again where they were cut
Cut only the mature trees, leave the young ones
Never set fire to the bush
Keep only as many animals as the land can feed; use paddocks
Use energy-saving stoves, biogas or gas instead of much firewood
Government marks off forest reserves and national parks and protects them by law
Keep the soil fertile so land is not cleared again and again

blocks.x: **What a pupil can do:** plant a tree at home and at school, water it, put a small fence round it, and never break young plants.

items: Saying vegetation means only trees — grass and crops are vegetation too.
Calling a planted forest a **natural** forest.
Writing "cutting trees" as a way of **caring** for vegetation.
Mixing up **afforestation** and **reafforestation**.
Giving a **use** when the question asks how people **destroy** vegetation.
Saying plants give us carbon dioxide — they give us **oxygen**.

What is natural vegetation?
What is planted vegetation?

How does vegetation help rain to form?
How do the roots of plants help the soil?

Give any three results of destroying vegetation.

**Forests, swamps, shrubs, grass and crops**
**Vegetation that grew on its own**, without being planted by people
**Vegetation planted and cared for by people**

**Planting trees where there were none before**
**Planting trees again where they had been cut**
**Cutting only the mature trees and leaving the young ones**
**Keeping too many animals on the same land** so the grass is eaten down to the roots

It means the government **marks it off by law** as a protected reserve.

blocks.x: *Curriculum reference: NCDC Primary Four Social Studies Syllabus, Term II, Topic 4 (15 periods, pages 26–31).*

**How to use this topic.** The syllabus asks about the people of **your own district** — their origin, why they settled there and the work they do. You fill in the tribes, clans and jobs of your own district.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: explain the origin of the people in your district
name the tribes and clans found in your district
tell a legend of one of those people
give the causes of immigration
give the factors that make people settle in a place
name the types of work people do and the problems they meet

blocks.x: The environment has two parts:

head: Physical environment
Social environment
rows: The natural things — land, water, air, plants, animals
**People and the things people make** — homes, schools, roads, markets

blocks.x: This topic is about the **social environment**: the people.

sections.title: 2. What is a tribe? What is a clan? What is a totem?

head: Word
Meaning
rows: A large group of people who share one language, one culture and one origin
A smaller group inside a tribe, whose members believe they came from one ancestor
A person from whom a family or clan came long ago
An animal or plant that a clan respects and does not eat
The whole way of life of a group of people

blocks.x: A **tribe is made up of many clans**. Each clan usually has its own **totem**.
**Fill this in for your own district:**

head: Question
My answer
rows: The main tribe or tribes in my district

sections.title: 3. What is a legend? Name the three legends in the syllabus.

blocks.x: A **legend** is an **old story handed down by word of mouth**, telling how a group of people began. Legends are told by elders. They are not history that can be proved, but they teach a people about themselves.

*The syllabus names these three legends but does not print the stories. Ask an elder, your teacher or the school library to tell you the one that belongs to your own people, and write it in your own words.*

sections.title: 4. What is migration? What do immigration and emigration mean?

head: Word
Meaning
rows: The movement of people from one place to another to settle
A person who moves into a place
A person who moves out of a place

blocks.x: **A way to remember: I**mmigration = coming **I**n.

head: Cause
Why people move
rows: To find enough water and grass for animals and food for the family
To find work and earn money
To escape a disease that is killing many people
To escape a long time without rain
To find good soil for growing crops

sections.title: 6. What is a drought? What is an epidemic?

head: Word
Meaning
rows: A disease that attacks very many people at once

sections.title: 7. What is a settlement pattern? What makes people settle in a place?

blocks.x: A **settlement pattern** is **the way people's homes are arranged in a place** — whether they are close together or far apart.

head: Factor
Why it attracts people
rows: Crops grow well, so there is food
People can buy and sell and earn money
Schools, water, good roads and health care are near

blocks.x: **Why some places have few people**
Poor or rocky soil · too little rain · steep slopes · thick forests · big swamps · insecurity · pests and diseases · no roads, schools or water.

sections.title: 8. What types of work do people do? Why do people work?

head: Work
What the person does
rows: Catches fish from lakes, rivers or ponds
Makes pots and jars from clay
Makes bricks and builds with them
Makes mats, baskets, carpets and carvings

blocks.x: An **occupation** is the work a person does to earn a living.
**Why people work:** to get food, to get money, to pay school fees, to buy clothes and medicine, to build a home, and to serve others.

sections.title: 9. What problems do people face in their work?

head: Problem
What it does
rows: People cannot work in safety and property is destroyed
Animals die, so the farmer loses money
Goods cannot reach the market, and they go bad

topics.subject: SST
topics.title: Our Leaders in the District
topics.heading: TOPIC 5: OUR LEADERS IN THE DISTRICT

blocks.x: *Curriculum reference: NCDC Primary Four Social Studies Syllabus, Term III, Topic 5 (25 periods, pages 31–35).*
**How to use this topic.** The syllabus asks about the leaders of **your own district**. You fill in the names of the leaders where you live.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: name the different groups of leaders in the district
say what each group of leaders does
describe the local council structure from LC1 to LC5
explain how leaders are chosen
describe how an election is carried out
say what makes a good leader

sections.title: 1. Who is a leader? Why do we need leaders?

blocks.x: A **leader** is a person who **guides, plans and organises other people** so that work is done well and people live in peace.
**Why we need leaders:** to keep law and order · to plan development · to settle quarrels · to speak for the people · to look after public property · to represent the people to government.

sections.title: 2. Name the four groups of leaders in a district.

blocks.x: (a) Political leaders
Chosen by the people, or appointed by government, to govern. **LC** means **Local Council**.

head: Leader
Where they work
rows: Looks after security in the district

blocks.x: (b) Civic leaders
These are **government officers**. They are **appointed** because of their training, not elected.

head: Leader
Work
rows: The head of all civil servants in the district
In charge of health services and hospitals
Advises farmers on crops and animals
Head of the police in the district

blocks.x: (c) Religious leaders
They lead people in worship and teach good behaviour.
**Bishops · priests · reverends · pastors · sheikhs · khadis.**
(d) Voluntary leaders
They lead **without being paid**, because they want to help.
**Scouts and Guides leaders · leaders of NGOs** such as **UWESO**, **TASO** and **the Red Cross**.
**UWESO** — Uganda Women's Effort to Save Orphans. **TASO** — The AIDS Support Organisation. These two are the syllabus's own examples of NGOs.
**Fill this in for your own district:**

head: Way
What it means
Example
rows: The people **vote** for the person they want
LC1 to LC5 chairpersons, Members of Parliament, class prefects
The RDC, the CAO, the District Health Officer
Cultural leaders — a king, a chief, a clan head
A person **offers himself or herself** to serve, unpaid
Scout leaders, Red Cross helpers, church group leaders

sections.title: 4. How is an election carried out?

head: Step
What happens
rows: Names of those old enough to vote are written on the **voters' register**

topics.title: How to Meet People's Needs in Our District
topics.heading: TOPIC 6: HOW TO MEET PEOPLE'S NEEDS IN OUR DISTRICT

blocks.x: *Curriculum reference: NCDC Primary Four Social Studies Syllabus, Term III, Topic 6 (25 periods, pages 35–40).*
**How to use this topic.** These notes teach you the services, who provides them, the problems met and the solutions. You name the actual centres in your own district.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: explain what social services are
name the types of social services in a district
name the people who provide social services and match each to the service
name the problems met in providing social services
suggest solutions to those problems
say how the social service centres should be cared for

sections.title: 1. What are social services? Who provides them?

blocks.x: **Social services** are the **things provided to help people live well**, which people cannot easily provide for themselves alone.

**Government has the responsibility of providing social services.** Government also allows some others to provide them on its behalf — **religious groups, private medical practitioners and business people**.

sections.title: 2. Name the types of social services.

head: Service
What it provides
Where it is found
rows: Police stations, police posts, army barracks
Roads, bus parks, taxi stages, landing sites
Boreholes, protected springs, taps, water tanks
Graders and road gangs at work
Post office, telephones, faxes, **e-mail and websites**

blocks.x: **Newer than the syllabus:** the syllabus (2010) lists **faxes** among the ways of communicating. Faxes are hardly used in Uganda today. **Mobile phones, mobile money and the internet** now do most of this work. The syllabus list is kept above because it is what the curriculum says, and the change is noted here.
A **service provider** is a person or group that gives a service.

head: Provider
Service they give
rows: Banking and safe keeping of money
Food, clothing, shelter, school fees, love and care

blocks.x: **Match each one:** *A doctor* → *treats the sick.* *A veterinary officer* → *treats animals.* *A carpenter* → *makes doors, desks and furniture.*

sections.title: 4. What problems are met in providing social services?

head: Problem
What it causes
rows: People cannot pay for services, and government has little money
Floods and drought spoil roads and crops
Hunger makes people weak and unable to work
Money meant for services is taken by dishonest people
People damage and do not look after what is provided
People waste time instead of working
Too many people for the few services there are
People do not do their work well

sections.title: 5. What are the solutions to these problems?

head: Problem
Suggested solution
rows: Start income-generating work · join savings groups · work hard · learn skills
Plant trees · irrigate · store food after harvest · build stronger roads
Grow more food crops · store food well · practise better farming
Guard property · report thieves · fence and lock the centres
Report corrupt officers · punish them by law · keep clear records
Teach people to care for public property · form user committees
Educate people on the dignity of work · create jobs
Family planning and education · build more schools and health centres
Train and supervise workers · reward good work

blocks.x: The syllabus also lists **providing medical services**, **controlling population growth** and **introducing group farming** among the solutions, and asks learners to plant short-term crops and draw posters on increasing food production.

sections.title: 6. How do we care for social service centres?

blocks.x: Social service centres belong to **all of us** — they are **public property**. Caring for them is everybody's work.

head: Centre
How to care for it
rows: Sweep and slash the compound · do not write on walls or break desks · use the latrine properly
Keep it clean · do not steal drugs · queue patiently
Keep the surroundings clean · repair the handle · do not wash clothes at the source
Clear the trenches · do not dig in the road · fill small potholes
Throw rubbish in the pit · do not damage the stalls
Report crime honestly · do not give false information

blocks.x: **What a P.4 pupil can do:** take part in cleaning the school and the road to it, report damage to a teacher, use water carefully, and tell others why these places matter.
**Road safety:** practise **safe ways of crossing the road** — **stop, look right, look left, look right again, and cross when it is clear**. Use a zebra crossing where there is one.

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Lack of enough money and basic things
Dishonest use of a position for personal gain
The number of people living in a place
Keeping something in good working order

Thinking only government must care for the centres — **everybody** must.
